Let \(q=p\). The answer is

\[
\boxed{p^7+5p^5-10p^4+5p^3-p^2-p+1}.
\]

**Solution.** Modulo the center \(Z(G)=\{(0,0,t)\}\), the commutator is

\[
[(u,v),(u',v')]=u\cdot v'-u'\cdot v .
\]

Thus an admissible subgroup \(A\) corresponds to a \(3\)-dimensional totally isotropic subspace \(W\subset \mathbb F_p^3\oplus \mathbb F_p^3\). The two transversality conditions say \(W\) is the graph of a linear map \(M:\mathbb F_p^3\to\mathbb F_p^3\):

\[
W=\{(u,Mu):u\in\mathbb F_p^3\}.
\]

The isotropic condition gives

\[
u\cdot M u'=u'\cdot M u,
\]

so \(M\) is symmetric. The diagonal-intersection condition says

\[
\dim\ker(M-I)=1.
\]

Therefore admissible subgroups are exactly symmetric \(3\times 3\) matrices \(M\) for which \(M-I\) has rank \(2\). The orthogonal group acts by

\[
M\mapsto QMQ^T.
\]

So we must count \(\mathcal O\)-orbits on ordered pairs \((M,N)\) of symmetric matrices with \(M-I,N-I\) both rank \(2\).

By Burnside, the desired number is

\[
\frac1{|\mathcal O|}\sum_{Q\in\mathcal O} f(Q)^2,
\]

where \(f(Q)\) is the number of rank-\(2\) symmetric matrices \(S\) satisfying \(QSQ^T=S\). Since \(|\mathcal O|=2q(q^2-1)\), it remains to compute \(f(Q)\) by conjugacy type.

For \(Q=\pm I\), every symmetric rank-\(2\) matrix is fixed. Its radical is one of \(q^2+q+1\) lines, and on the quotient there are \(q^2(q-1)\) nondegenerate symmetric \(2\times 2\) matrices. Thus

\[
A=f(\pm I)=q^2(q-1)(q^2+q+1).
\]

For a reflection or negative reflection, the space splits as \(1\oplus 2\), so a fixed symmetric matrix is block diagonal. Rank \(2\) occurs either as \(0\oplus\text{rank }2\), or as nonzero scalar \(\oplus\text{rank }1\). Hence

\[
B=(q^2(q-1))+(q-1)(q^2-1)=(q-1)(2q^2-1).
\]

There are \(2q^2\) such elements, since reflections correspond to anisotropic lines and there are \(q^2\) of those.

For nontrivial unipotent elements, the self-adjoint commutant contains no rank-\(2\) element. In a Jordan basis, a commuting operator has form \(xI+yN+zN^2\), and self-adjointness forces \(y=0\). Then the rank is \(3,1,\) or \(0\), never \(2\). There are \(2(q^2-1)\) unipotent or negative-unipotent elements.

All remaining elements are semisimple rotations. On the \(2\)-dimensional orthogonal complement of the fixed line, self-adjointness forces the commuting part to be scalar, so rank \(2\) occurs exactly when the line part is \(0\) and the plane scalar is nonzero. Thus

\[
f(Q)=q-1
\]

for the remaining

\[
2q(q^2-1)-2-2q^2-2(q^2-1)=2q(q^2-2q-1)
\]

elements.

Burnside gives

\[
\frac{
2A^2+2q^2B^2+2q(q^2-2q-1)(q-1)^2
}{
2q(q^2-1)
}.
\]

Substituting \(A=q^2(q-1)(q^2+q+1)\) and \(B=(q-1)(2q^2-1)\), this simplifies to

\[
q^7+5q^5-10q^4+5q^3-q^2-q+1.
\]

Restoring \(q=p\), the number of orbits is

\[
\boxed{p^7+5p^5-10p^4+5p^3-p^2-p+1}.
\]
